x-m-e4-01.title: The Key Number Puzzle
x-m-e4-01.goal: Make large numbers that meet several clues at the same time, and judge whether the clues decide the number as just one.
x-m-e4-01.material: The key number of the treasure chest is an 8-digit number. There are only three clues. Clue 1: The digit in the ten-millions place is 5. Clue 2: The digit in the hundred-thousands place is 0. Clue 3: The digit in the ten-thousands place is greater than the digit in the ten-millions place.
x-m-e4-01.thinking.0: Making a number that meets several clues at the same time
x-m-e4-01.thinking.1: Telling apart the name of a place from the digit in that place
x-m-e4-01.thinking.2: Judging whether the clues are enough
x-m-e4-01.prereq.0: Reading and writing numbers up to the ten-millions
x-m-e4-01.prereq.1: Knows the place names ones, tens, hundreds, thousands, ten-thousands, hundred-thousands, millions, and ten-millions
x-m-e4-01.s.s1.prompt: If you read Clue 3 together with Clue 1, what can you tell about the digit in the ten-thousands place?
x-m-e4-01.s.s1.hint.0: Clue 3 compares 'the digit in the ten-thousands place' with 'the digit in the ten-millions place.' The digit in the ten-millions place is given in Clue 1.
x-m-e4-01.s.s1.hint.1: Write out the single digits that are greater than 5, one at a time.
x-m-e4-01.s.s1.o.a: The digit in the ten-thousands place is one of 0, 1, 2, 3, 4
x-m-e4-01.s.s1.r.a: You read 'greater than' backward as 'less than.' Check the direction of the inequality sign again.
x-m-e4-01.s.s1.o.b: The digit in the ten-thousands place can be anything if it is 5 or more
x-m-e4-01.s.s1.r.b: If you allow 5 too, the case of 'equal' gets mixed in. Think about whether 5 is included in 'greater than.'
x-m-e4-01.s.s1.o.c: The digit in the ten-thousands place is one of 6, 7, 8, 9
x-m-e4-01.s.s1.r.c: You took the digit in the ten-millions place from Clue 1 and connected it to Clue 3.
x-m-e4-01.s.s1.explain: The digit in the ten-millions place is 5, so the digits greater than that are 6, 7, 8, 9. You can only find this by reading the two clues together.
x-m-e4-01.s.s2.prompt: Make 2 different 8-digit numbers that meet all three clues. (key number n)
x-m-e4-01.s.s2.hint.0: First write the digits in the ten-millions place and the hundred-thousands place as the clues say.
x-m-e4-01.s.s2.hint.1: Decide which digits can go in the ten-thousands place.
x-m-e4-01.s.s2.hint.2: After you fill in the remaining places, read the clues again for each place to check.
x-m-e4-01.s.s2.fail.c1: It is not an 8-digit number (a natural number from ten million up to but not including one hundred million).
x-m-e4-01.s.s2.ok.c2: The digit in the ten-millions place is 5.
x-m-e4-01.s.s2.fail.c2: The digit in the ten-millions place is not 5.
x-m-e4-01.s.s2.ok.c3: The digit in the hundred-thousands place is 0.
x-m-e4-01.s.s2.fail.c3: The digit in the hundred-thousands place is not 0.
x-m-e4-01.s.s2.ok.c4: The digit in the ten-thousands place is greater than the digit in the ten-millions place.
x-m-e4-01.s.s2.fail.c4: The digit in the ten-thousands place is not greater than the digit in the ten-millions place.
x-m-e4-01.s.s2.explain: For example, 50,070,000 and 50,090,123 both follow all three clues. The clues say nothing about the millions, thousands, hundreds, tens, and ones places, so the answer is not decided as just one.
x-m-e4-01.s.s2.because.prompt: Is there only one candidate for the key number, or are there many? Explain by connecting it to the places the clues do not mention.
x-m-e4-01.s.s2.because.hint.0: Compare the two numbers you made and see which places are different.
x-m-e4-01.s.s2.because.hint.1: Mark which place each of the three clues is talking about.
x-m-e4-01.s.s2.because.placeholder: Example: The places the clues do not mention are ...
x-m-e4-01.s.s2.because.selfAssess.0: Did you say in which place your two numbers are different?
x-m-e4-01.s.s2.because.selfAssess.1: Did you write 'places we do not know' and 'places decided by the clues' separately?
x-m-e4-01.s.s2.because.model.0: There are many. The clues only talk about the ten-millions, hundred-thousands, and ten-thousands places, and do not tell us the millions, thousands, hundreds, tens, and ones places, so any digit can go there.
x-m-e4-01.s.s2.because.model.1: There is not just one. The other places have no clues, so they can change from 0 to 9, which is why 50070000 works and 50090123 works too.

x-m-e4-02.title: Where Did It Go Wrong When Changing to Digits?
x-m-e4-02.goal: Find the wrong line in a solution that changes a large number read in words into digits, and fix it using the 0s in the places that were not read.
x-m-e4-02.material: Minseo wrote a solution to write 'three thousand twenty-five ten-thousand, four thousand six' in digits.
x-m-e4-02.thinking.0: Finding the wrong line in a solution
x-m-e4-02.thinking.1: Checking that the words read match the place values
x-m-e4-02.prereq.0: Reading and writing numbers up to the ten-thousands
x-m-e4-02.prereq.1: Knows the name of each place and the role of 0
x-m-e4-02.s.s1.prompt: Pick the first wrong line in Minseo's solution.
x-m-e4-02.s.s1.hint.0: For each line, check one by one whether 'the words read' and 'the digits written' match.
x-m-e4-02.s.s1.hint.1: From 'four thousand six,' say the digit in the thousands place and the digit in the ones place first.
x-m-e4-02.s.s1.line.0: Let's write 'three thousand twenty-five ten-thousand, four thousand six' in digits.
x-m-e4-02.s.s1.line.1: The three thousand twenty-five before 'ten-thousand' is 3025. Since it is in units of ten-thousand, put 4 zeros after it to get 30250000.
x-m-e4-02.s.s1.line.2: The four thousand six after 'ten-thousand' is 4 and 6, so write them together as 46.
x-m-e4-02.s.s1.line.4: So three thousand twenty-five ten-thousand, four thousand six is 30,250,046.
x-m-e4-02.s.s1.explain: Line 3 is the first wrong place. In four thousand six, the thousands place is 4 and the ones place is 6, and the hundreds and tens places were not read but are 0, so it is 4006. Lines 4 and 5 are wrong because they carry on the wrong value from line 3.
x-m-e4-02.s.s2.prompt: Fix line 3 correctly and write the correct final number. Also explain why the first value was wrong.
x-m-e4-02.s.s2.hint.0: Read 'four thousand six' aloud and mark the places you read.
x-m-e4-02.s.s2.hint.1: Think about what should go in the places that were not read.
x-m-e4-02.s.s2.selfAssess.0: Can you say the digits in the thousands, hundreds, tens, and ones places of your corrected value one at a time?
x-m-e4-02.s.s2.selfAssess.1: Did you write in your own words why a place needs a 0 even if you do not say it when reading?
x-m-e4-02.s.s2.model.0: Four thousand six must be 4006. The hundreds place and the tens place were not read, but there must be 0s, so the final number is 30,254,006.
x-m-e4-02.s.s2.model.1: It is not 46 but 4006. The thousands place is 4, and the hundreds and tens places are empty places, so I have to write 0s. So it becomes 30254006.

x-m-e4-03.title: Doyun's 'Special Triangle'
x-m-e4-03.goal: Judge a claim using measurement error and the sum of the three angles of a triangle, and make the three angles of a triangle that fits the conditions yourself.
x-m-e4-03.material: Doyun measured the three angles of a triangle-shaped piece of paper with a protractor and got 58°, 62°, and 63°. Then Doyun said, 'The sum of the three angles is not 180°, so this is a special triangle!'
x-m-e4-03.thinking.0: Thinking through possible causes when a measured value and a property do not match
x-m-e4-03.thinking.1: Making angle sizes that meet the conditions
x-m-e4-03.thinking.2: Explaining why there cannot be two obtuse angles
x-m-e4-03.prereq.0: Measuring angles with a protractor and telling apart acute, right, and obtuse angles
x-m-e4-03.prereq.1: What you learned about the sum of the sizes of the three angles of a triangle
x-m-e4-03.s.s1.prompt: What is the best way to take Doyun's measured values and claim?
x-m-e4-03.s.s1.hint.0: Add up the sizes of all three angles.
x-m-e4-03.s.s1.hint.1: Think of the places where a measurement with a protractor easily goes off (where you read the scale, when the sides of the angle are short).
x-m-e4-03.s.s1.o.a: The sum of the three angles is different from triangle to triangle, and this is the evidence, so it is right that this triangle is 183°
x-m-e4-03.s.s1.r.a: One measured value, measured once, cannot change the properties of all triangles. It is also necessary to doubt the measured value.
x-m-e4-03.s.s1.o.b: Measurements made with a protractor can be a little off, so measure again and check other triangles too
x-m-e4-03.s.s1.o.c: The sum is 3° too big, so take 3° off the largest angle, rewrite it, and finish
x-m-e4-03.s.s1.r.c: If you rewrite values to fit the conclusion, you cannot tell where the measuring went wrong. Measuring again comes first.
x-m-e4-03.s.s1.explain: The sum of the three angles, 58+62+63, is 183°. It is common to be off by about 1° to 3° when reading a protractor's scale. So measuring again or checking with other triangles is the right thing to do.
x-m-e4-03.s.s2.prompt: Make 2 triangles in which all three angles are different and one is an obtuse angle, with different sizes of the three angles. (three angles a, b, c; unit is degrees)
x-m-e4-03.s.s2.hint.0: First decide the size of the one obtuse angle.
x-m-e4-03.s.s2.hint.1: Think about what the sum of the other two angles has to be.
x-m-e4-03.s.s2.hint.2: Split it into two other angles that are different from each other and both greater than 0.
x-m-e4-03.s.s2.ok.c1: All three angles are greater than 0.
x-m-e4-03.s.s2.fail.c1: The size of an angle must be greater than 0.
x-m-e4-03.s.s2.ok.c2: The sum of the three angles is 180°.
x-m-e4-03.s.s2.fail.c2: The sum of the three angles is not 180°.
x-m-e4-03.s.s2.ok.c3: There is an angle greater than 90° (an obtuse angle).
x-m-e4-03.s.s2.fail.c3: There is no obtuse angle (an angle greater than 90°).
x-m-e4-03.s.s2.fail.c4: There are angles of the same size.
x-m-e4-03.s.s2.explain: For example, 100°, 50°, 30° and 120°, 40°, 20° each add up to 180° and each has one obtuse angle. Triangles with the same angles in a different order count as the same triangle.
x-m-e4-03.s.s2.because.prompt: Using numbers, explain why a triangle cannot have two obtuse angles.
x-m-e4-03.s.s2.because.hint.0: Think about whether the size of one obtuse angle is greater or less than 90°.
x-m-e4-03.s.s2.because.hint.1: Check what number two obtuse angles would add up to more than.
x-m-e4-03.s.s2.because.placeholder: Example: An obtuse angle is greater than 90°, so ...
x-m-e4-03.s.s2.because.selfAssess.0: Did you say, using numbers, that the sum of two obtuse angles is greater than 180°?
x-m-e4-03.s.s2.because.selfAssess.1: Did you also think about what happens to the remaining angle?
x-m-e4-03.s.s2.because.model.0: An obtuse angle is greater than 90°, so two obtuse angles add up to more than 180°, and the sum of the three angles cannot be 180°.
x-m-e4-03.s.s2.because.model.1: Even if just one obtuse angle is 100°, only 80° is left for the sum of the other two angles. An obtuse angle goes over 90°, so two of them would go over 180°, which is not allowed.

x-m-e4-04.title: What Should We Ask to Find Angle ㄷ?
x-m-e4-04.goal: Use the properties of an isosceles triangle and the sum of the three angles to sort out what information lets you find one angle and what information is not enough.
x-m-e4-04.material: In triangle ㄱㄴㄷ, side ㄱㄴ and side ㄱㄷ are the same length. In an isosceles triangle, the angles opposite the two sides of the same length, angle ㄴ and angle ㄷ, are the same size. Jisu will receive just one piece of information from a friend and try to find the size of angle ㄷ.
x-m-e4-04.thinking.1: Making possible cases yourself when information is not enough
x-m-e4-04.thinking.2: Saying what more information is needed
x-m-e4-04.prereq.0: What you learned about the sum of the sizes of the three angles of a triangle
x-m-e4-04.prereq.1: The meaning of an isosceles triangle
x-m-e4-04.s.s1.prompt: Choose all the cases where the one piece of information a friend gives is enough to find the size of angle ㄷ.
x-m-e4-04.s.s1.hint.0: To know angle ㄷ, first think about how angle ㄴ and angle ㄷ are related.
x-m-e4-04.s.s1.hint.1: For each choice, check 'does that information decide one value?'
x-m-e4-04.s.s1.o.a: The size of angle ㄴ is 50°
x-m-e4-04.s.s1.o.b: The length of side ㄴㄷ is 6 cm
x-m-e4-04.s.s1.r.b: The length of a side alone does not decide the size of an angle. Even with a side of the same length, both a pointy triangle and a flat triangle are possible.
x-m-e4-04.s.s1.o.c: The size of angle ㄱ is 80°
x-m-e4-04.s.s1.r.c: Knowing only angle ㄱ, you can decide the rest using the sum of the three angles and the fact that two angles are the same.
x-m-e4-04.s.s1.o.d: Angle ㄱ is an acute angle
x-m-e4-04.s.s1.r.d: 'Acute angle' only tells you a range of sizes. It does not decide an exact value.
x-m-e4-04.s.s1.explain: If angle ㄴ is 50°, angle ㄷ is also 50°. If angle ㄱ is 80°, the other two angles add up to 100° and the two angles are the same, so angle ㄷ is 50°. The length of side ㄴㄷ or the word 'acute' alone does not decide angle ㄷ.
x-m-e4-04.s.s2.prompt: Now suppose you do not know that triangle ㄱㄴㄷ is an isosceles triangle. With only the information that angle ㄴ is 50°, make 2 triangles in which angle ㄷ has different values. (angle ㄱ = a, angle ㄷ = c, unit is degrees)
x-m-e4-04.s.s2.hint.0: After taking away angle ㄴ, what must the sum of the other two angles be?
x-m-e4-04.s.s2.hint.1: Decide angle ㄱ first, then fit angle ㄷ.
x-m-e4-04.s.s2.hint.2: The values of angle ㄷ must be different.
x-m-e4-04.s.s2.fail.c1: The size of an angle must be greater than 0.
x-m-e4-04.s.s2.ok.c2: The sum of the three angles (including angle ㄴ at 50°) is 180°.
x-m-e4-04.s.s2.fail.c2: The sum of the three angles is not 180°.
x-m-e4-04.s.s2.explain: Even when angle ㄴ is 50°, all that is needed is that the sum of angle ㄱ and angle ㄷ is 130°. Angle ㄷ can have many values, like 80° and 50°, or 30° and 100°, so angle ㄴ alone cannot decide angle ㄷ.
x-m-e4-04.s.s2.because.prompt: Write why angle ㄷ is not decided as one value, and what more information you would need to know to decide angle ㄷ.
x-m-e4-04.s.s2.because.hint.0: Compare the sum of angle ㄱ and angle ㄷ in the two triangles you made.
x-m-e4-04.s.s2.because.hint.1: Think about what one more thing you would need to know to decide angle ㄷ.
x-m-e4-04.s.s2.because.placeholder: Example: If you only know angle ㄴ, ...
x-m-e4-04.s.s2.because.selfAssess.0: Can you say that angle ㄷ in your two triangles has different values?
x-m-e4-04.s.s2.because.selfAssess.1: Can you explain why the information 'it is an isosceles triangle' helps?
x-m-e4-04.s.s2.because.model.0: If angle ㄴ is 50°, all that is needed is that angle ㄱ and angle ㄷ add up to 130°, so there are many possibilities. You need to know one more thing, angle ㄱ or angle ㄷ.
x-m-e4-04.s.s2.because.model.1: The other two angles add up to 130°, so 80° and 50° work, and 30° and 100° work too. If you also had the information that it is an isosceles triangle, you could tell.

x-m-e4-05.title: Guessing the Name of the Secret Quadrilateral
x-m-e4-05.goal: As clues increase, correct the name of the shape more precisely, and tell apart whether your first answer was wrong or just less precise.
x-m-e4-05.material: There is a secret quadrilateral. The clues are revealed one at a time. Think about the names trapezoid, parallelogram, rhombus, rectangle, and square.
x-m-e4-05.thinking.0: Narrowing down the shape by collecting clues
x-m-e4-05.thinking.2: Understanding the inclusion relationships between shapes
x-m-e4-05.prereq.0: The meanings of trapezoid (a quadrilateral that has even just one pair of parallel sides), parallelogram, rhombus, rectangle, and square
x-m-e4-05.prereq.1: What you learned about the sum of the sizes of the four angles of a quadrilateral
x-m-e4-05.s.s1.prompt: Each time a clue is revealed, choose the name you can say right now.
x-m-e4-05.s.s1.hint.0: Check whether the revealed clue clashes with the conditions of the name you have settled on so far.
x-m-e4-05.s.s1.hint.1: Write out the conditions of the shape one at a time and compare what the new clue adds to those conditions.
x-m-e4-05.s.s1.st.0.info: Clue 1: Both pairs of opposite sides are parallel.
x-m-e4-05.s.s1.st.0.ask: What is the best thing you can say right now?
x-m-e4-05.s.s1.st.0.after: If there are two pairs of parallel sides, it is a parallelogram. If there is even one pair of parallel sides, it is a trapezoid, so trapezoid is also a correct thing to say, but parallelogram is more precise. We do not yet know whether it is a rhombus or a rectangle.
x-m-e4-05.s.s1.st.0.o.a: We can decide it is a rhombus
x-m-e4-05.s.s1.st.0.r.a: Two pairs of parallel sides alone do not tell you whether the sides are the same length.
x-m-e4-05.s.s1.st.0.o.b: It is a parallelogram. It might be a rectangle or a rhombus
x-m-e4-05.s.s1.st.0.r.b: This is said to fit the meaning of two pairs of parallel sides, and it leaves open what we do not yet know.
x-m-e4-05.s.s1.st.0.o.c: We can decide it is a rectangle
x-m-e4-05.s.s1.st.0.r.c: There is not yet a clue about whether the angles are right angles.
x-m-e4-05.s.s1.st.1.info: Clue 2: All four angles are the same size.
x-m-e4-05.s.s1.st.1.ask: Now what name can you say?
x-m-e4-05.s.s1.st.1.after: The four angles are all the same and add up to 360°, so each is 90°. A parallelogram with four right angles is a rectangle. We do not know the lengths of the sides yet, so we cannot say it is a square.
x-m-e4-05.s.s1.st.1.o.a: It is a rectangle. If the four angles are the same, each is 360°÷4=90°
x-m-e4-05.s.s1.st.1.r.a: This connected the sum of the four angles with 'all the same' to reach right angles.
x-m-e4-05.s.s1.st.1.o.b: It is a rhombus. If the angles are all the same, the sides must be all the same too
x-m-e4-05.s.s1.st.1.r.b: Angles being the same and sides being the same are different things.
x-m-e4-05.s.s1.st.1.o.c: It is a square. Because the angles are all the same
x-m-e4-05.s.s1.st.1.r.c: We do not yet know the lengths of the sides, but this decided it is a square.
x-m-e4-05.s.s1.st.2.info: Clue 3: Two neighboring sides are the same length.
x-m-e4-05.s.s1.st.2.ask: What is the most precise name, and what is the right judgment about the 'parallelogram' you said at first?
x-m-e4-05.s.s1.st.2.after: It is a parallelogram, it has right angles, and neighboring sides are the same length, so it is a square. A square also meets the conditions of a parallelogram, so the first answer was not wrong; it was less precise.
x-m-e4-05.s.s1.st.2.o.a: It is a rhombus. Even with right angles, a rhombus is different from a square
x-m-e4-05.s.s1.st.2.r.a: Even with right angles it can be a rhombus, and a square has the conditions of both. See whether there is a more precise name.
x-m-e4-05.s.s1.st.2.o.b: It is a square. A square is not a parallelogram, so the first answer was wrong
x-m-e4-05.s.s1.st.2.r.b: A square also has two pairs of parallel opposite sides. It meets the conditions of a parallelogram as they are.
x-m-e4-05.s.s1.st.2.o.c: It is a square. The parallelogram I said first was not a wrong thing to say either
x-m-e4-05.s.s1.st.2.o.d: It is a rectangle. The lengths of the sides are not needed to decide the name
x-m-e4-05.s.s1.st.2.r.d: The clue that the sides are the same length narrows the name down further.
x-m-e4-05.s.s1.reflect: As the clues increased, how did your answer change? How can you tell apart when your first answer becomes 'wrong' and when it becomes 'less precise'?
x-m-e4-05.s.s2.prompt: Which is the best idea about 'A square may be called a rectangle'?
x-m-e4-05.s.s2.hint.0: First write the meaning of a rectangle in one sentence.
x-m-e4-05.s.s2.hint.1: Check one by one whether a square meets all the conditions in that sentence.
x-m-e4-05.s.s2.o.a: It may be called one. A square also meets the meaning of a rectangle, 'all four angles are right angles'
x-m-e4-05.s.s2.o.b: No. A rectangle must have a length and a width that are different
x-m-e4-05.s.s2.r.b: The meaning of a rectangle has no condition that 'the length and the width must be different.' Look again at what the conditions in the meaning are.
x-m-e4-05.s.s2.o.c: No. A square has its own name, so it is a completely different shape
x-m-e4-05.s.s2.r.c: Having its own name does not mean it fails to meet the conditions of another shape. Compare the conditions.
x-m-e4-05.s.s2.explain: A rectangle is a quadrilateral whose four angles are all right angles. A square has four right angles, so it meets the meaning of a rectangle. It just has one more condition: all the sides are the same length.

x-m-e4-06.title: Checking Seohyeon's Explanation
x-m-e4-06.goal: Find the logic error in the explanation 'If all four sides are the same, it is a square,' and explain a quadrilateral that is a counterexample.
x-m-e4-06.material: Seohyeon explained this to a friend. There is a mistake in this explanation.
x-m-e4-06.thinking.0: Finding where the explanation's logic is said backward
x-m-e4-06.thinking.2: Saying the conditions needed for it to hold
x-m-e4-06.prereq.0: The meanings of square, rhombus, and rectangle
x-m-e4-06.prereq.1: The meaning of a right angle
x-m-e4-06.s.s1.prompt: Pick the first wrong line in Seohyeon's explanation.
x-m-e4-06.s.s1.hint.0: Lines 1 and 2 talk about properties that a square has. Compare how the direction of what is said changes in line 3.
x-m-e4-06.s.s1.hint.1: Test with another example you know whether 'If A, then B' and 'If B, then A' say the same thing.
x-m-e4-06.s.s1.line.0: A square has four sides that are all the same length.
x-m-e4-06.s.s1.line.1: A square has four angles that are all right angles.
x-m-e4-06.s.s1.line.2: So every quadrilateral whose four sides are all the same length is a square.
x-m-e4-06.s.s1.line.3: A rhombus also has four sides of the same length, so it is a square.
x-m-e4-06.s.s1.explain: Line 3 is the first wrong place. Just because a square has four equal sides does not mean that, the other way around, 'if the four sides are equal, it is a square.' Line 4 carries on the wrong statement from line 3.
x-m-e4-06.s.s2.prompt: You want to show Seohyeon that this statement is not right. Give and explain an example of a quadrilateral whose four sides are all the same length but that is not a square.
x-m-e4-06.s.s2.hint.0: Think about what changes if you keep the four side lengths the same and press the shape down a little.
x-m-e4-06.s.s2.hint.1: To be a square, what else is needed besides the side lengths?
x-m-e4-06.s.s2.placeholder: Example: Even if the four sides are the same, ...
x-m-e4-06.s.s2.selfAssess.0: In your example, did you say both that the four sides are the same length and that the angles are not right angles?
x-m-e4-06.s.s2.selfAssess.1: Did you say that 'to be a square, both conditions are needed'?
x-m-e4-06.s.s2.model.0: A square has four equal sides, but not every shape with four equal sides is a square. If you press a rhombus so it leans, the sides stay the same but the angles are not right angles, so it is not a square.
x-m-e4-06.s.s2.model.1: Squash a quadrilateral whose four sides are all 5 cm. The side lengths are the same, but the four angles are not right angles, so it is not a square. A square must have equal sides and all right angles.

x-m-e4-07.title: Adding Fractions by Thinking About Pizza Slices
x-m-e4-07.goal: Explain, using 'the number of slices of the same size,' why you must not add the denominators when adding fractions with the same denominator.
x-m-e4-07.material: A pizza is cut into 5 slices of the same size. Minho first ate 2 slices and then ate 1 more slice. Jia said, '2/5 plus 1/5 is 3/10. You just add the numerators and also add the denominators.'
x-m-e4-07.thinking.1: Explaining using the meaning of a fraction (how many unit fractions)
x-m-e4-07.thinking.2: Saying the reason a rule is wrong
x-m-e4-07.prereq.0: The meaning of a fraction (how many of the equal parts a whole is divided into)
x-m-e4-07.prereq.1: Comparing the sizes of fractions with the same denominator
x-m-e4-07.s.s1.prompt: Choose all the reasons that show Jia's answer 3/10 is not right.
x-m-e4-07.s.s1.hint.0: Think about whether the size of one slice changed while eating.
x-m-e4-07.s.s1.hint.1: Compare how many slices the whole pizza is cut into for 3/10 and for 3/5.
x-m-e4-07.s.s1.o.a: When adding fractions, you must add both the numerators and the denominators to show the combined amount exactly
x-m-e4-07.s.s1.r.a: If you add the denominators, the size of the slices changes. Think again about what the denominator shows.
x-m-e4-07.s.s1.o.b: The slices eaten are each 1/5 of the pizza, so putting 2 slices and 1 slice together makes 3 slices of the same size
x-m-e4-07.s.s1.o.c: Adding always makes the denominator bigger, so it is natural that adding 1/5 to 2/5 makes the denominator 10
x-m-e4-07.s.s1.r.c: There is no evidence in this situation that adding fractions makes the denominator bigger. Check whether the size of the slices changed.
x-m-e4-07.s.s1.o.d: 3/10 is an amount where one pizza is cut into 10 slices, but this pizza is cut into 5 slices
x-m-e4-07.s.s1.explain: The slices eaten are each the size of 1/5, so 2 slices + 1 slice = 3 slices, that is, 3/5. 3/10 is one pizza cut into 10 slices, but this pizza is cut into 5 slices, so it is not right.
x-m-e4-07.s.s2.prompt: Explain to Jia in words, without a picture. What is 2/5 plus 1/5, and why does the denominator stay the same?
x-m-e4-07.s.s2.hint.0: Think about whether the size of the pizza slices changed while eating.
x-m-e4-07.s.s2.hint.1: Count how many 1/5s have come together.
x-m-e4-07.s.s2.placeholder: Example: The slices eaten are all ...
x-m-e4-07.s.s2.selfAssess.0: Did you use the words 'the size of the slices stays the same' or say the same meaning in another way?
x-m-e4-07.s.s2.selfAssess.1: Did you explain in your own words what the denominator shows?
x-m-e4-07.s.s2.model.0: If you eat 2 slices from a pizza cut into 5 slices and then eat 1 more slice, you ate 3 slices, so it is 3/5. The slice size stays the same, so the denominator 5 stays the same.
x-m-e4-07.s.s2.model.1: If you have two 1/5s and one 1/5, that is three 1/5s in all. So it is 3/5. The denominator tells how many equal parts the whole is cut into, so it does not change.

x-m-e4-08.title: Making Subtractions with a Difference of 1 and 3/7
x-m-e4-08.goal: Think backward to make several mixed-number subtractions that need regrouping and have a set difference, and explain why regrouping is needed.
x-m-e4-08.material: There are two mixed numbers with denominator 7. When you subtract the smaller from the larger, the difference is 1 and 3/7. You will make a subtraction in which you cannot subtract the fraction parts right away, so you have to change 1 from the whole number into a fraction.
x-m-e4-08.thinking.1: Making several examples that meet a condition (regrouping)
x-m-e4-08.thinking.2: Recognizing cases where the fraction parts cannot be subtracted
x-m-e4-08.prereq.0: Subtracting mixed numbers with the same denominator
x-m-e4-08.prereq.1: The meanings of proper fraction and mixed number
x-m-e4-08.s.s1.prompt: You want to subtract 2 and 6/7 from 4 and 2/7. How should you think when calculating the fraction part?
x-m-e4-08.s.s1.hint.0: First compare the fraction part of the number you subtract from with the fraction part of the number you subtract.
x-m-e4-08.s.s1.hint.1: Think about how you can change 4 into 3 plus some fraction.
x-m-e4-08.s.s1.o.a: For the fraction part, you must subtract the smaller from the larger, so subtract 2/7 from 6/7
x-m-e4-08.s.s1.r.a: If you swap the number you subtract and the number you subtract from, it becomes a different calculation. Check again what is being subtracted from 4 and 2/7.
x-m-e4-08.s.s1.o.b: If the fraction part is not enough, the answer becomes less than 0, so this subtraction cannot be done
x-m-e4-08.s.s1.r.b: If the whole number part has some to spare, it can fill in the fraction that is short. Compare the whole values.
x-m-e4-08.s.s1.o.c: You cannot subtract 6/7 from the fraction part 2/7, so change 1 in the whole number 4 into 7/7
x-m-e4-08.s.s1.explain: 4 and 2/7 is the same as 3 and 9/7. Subtracting 6/7 from 9/7 gives 3/7, and subtracting 2 from 3 gives 1, so the difference is 1 and 3/7.
x-m-e4-08.s.s2.prompt: Make 2 different subtractions with a difference of 1 and 3/7 in which you cannot subtract the fraction parts right away. (larger number: whole number aw, numerator an / smaller number: whole number bw, numerator bn, all denominators are 7)
x-m-e4-08.s.s2.hint.0: First decide the smaller number, then add 1 and 3/7 to it to make the larger number.
x-m-e4-08.s.s2.hint.1: See what happens when the fraction part goes over 7/7 after you add.
x-m-e4-08.s.s2.hint.2: Check whether the numerator of the larger number is smaller than the numerator of the smaller number.
x-m-e4-08.s.s2.var.aw: Whole number of the larger number
x-m-e4-08.s.s2.var.bw: Whole number of the smaller number
x-m-e4-08.s.s2.fail.c1: You can only write natural numbers.
x-m-e4-08.s.s2.ok.c2: The numerators and whole number parts of the mixed numbers are fine.
x-m-e4-08.s.s2.fail.c2: The numerator must be from 1 to 6, and the whole number part must be at least 1.
x-m-e4-08.s.s2.ok.c4: You cannot subtract the fraction parts right away (regrouping is needed).
x-m-e4-08.s.s2.fail.c4: You can subtract the fraction parts right away, so regrouping is not needed.
x-m-e4-08.s.s2.explain: Like 4 and 2/7 − 2 and 6/7 = 1 and 3/7, and 5 and 1/7 − 3 and 5/7 = 1 and 3/7, regrouping is needed only when the numerator of the larger number is smaller than the numerator of the smaller number.
x-m-e4-08.s.s2.because.prompt: Pick one subtraction you made and write why you cannot subtract the fraction parts right away and how the result becomes 1 and 3/7.
x-m-e4-08.s.s2.because.hint.0: Compare the two numerators of the fraction parts in your number sentence.
x-m-e4-08.s.s2.because.hint.1: Think about how many sevenths one whole number can be changed into.
x-m-e4-08.s.s2.because.placeholder: Example: If you look at the numerators of the fraction parts, ...
x-m-e4-08.s.s2.because.selfAssess.0: Did you compare the two numerators in your number sentence and say why regrouping is needed?
x-m-e4-08.s.s2.because.selfAssess.1: After changing, did you subtract the fraction parts and the whole number parts separately and check that you get 1 and 3/7?
x-m-e4-08.s.s2.because.model.0: When you subtract 2 and 6/7 from 4 and 2/7, you cannot subtract 6 from 2 in the fraction part. So change 1 in the whole number 4 into 7/7 to make 3 and 9/7, then 9 minus 6 is 3 and 3 minus 2 is 1, so it is 1 and 3/7.
x-m-e4-08.s.s2.because.model.1: When you subtract 3 and 5/7 from 5 and 1/7, the numerator 1 is smaller than 5, so you cannot subtract right away. So change 1 in the whole number 5 into 7/7 to make 4 and 8/7, then 8 minus 5 is 3 and 4 minus 3 is 1, so it is 1 and 3/7.

x-m-e4-09.title: The Tangerine Bars Are the Same Length, but Are the Numbers of Students the Same Too?
x-m-e4-09.goal: Know that you must check the value of one unit of the scale when comparing bar graphs, and make a case in which two graphs with different scales give the same number of students.
x-m-e4-09.material: Class 가 and Class 나 each surveyed the fruits they like and showed them in bar graphs. In the two graphs, the tangerine bars look the same length to the eye. Jiho said, 'The bars are the same length, so the number of students who like tangerines is the same in both classes.' You have not yet checked how many students one unit of the scale stands for in each graph.
x-m-e4-09.thinking.0: Sorting out the information needed for the comparison
x-m-e4-09.thinking.1: Showing the same number by using the scale unit
x-m-e4-09.thinking.2: Saying the risk of comparing by bar length alone
x-m-e4-09.prereq.0: Reading the scale on a bar graph and knowing the number one unit stands for
x-m-e4-09.prereq.1: Multiplication facts and multiplying two-digit numbers
x-m-e4-09.s.s1.prompt: Choose all the information you absolutely need to compare the numbers of students who like tangerines in the two classes.
x-m-e4-09.s.s1.hint.0: First say how you read the number of students from one graph.
x-m-e4-09.s.s1.hint.1: Check whether the information you chose decides the number of students.
x-m-e4-09.s.s1.o.a: How many students are in each of the two classes in all
x-m-e4-09.s.s1.r.a: The total number of students is needed when you compare 'rates.' This question is about how many students like tangerines.
x-m-e4-09.s.s1.o.b: How many students one unit of the scale stands for in each graph
x-m-e4-09.s.s1.o.c: Which fruit has the shortest bar, and how many units it has
x-m-e4-09.s.s1.r.c: The bars for other fruits do not change the number of students for tangerines. Think only about the tangerine bar.
x-m-e4-09.s.s1.o.d: How many units of the scale the tangerine bar goes up to
x-m-e4-09.s.s1.explain: You can find the number of students as 'the number one unit stands for × the number of units the bar goes up.' You need both the value of one unit and the number of units of the tangerine bar. The total number of students or the bars of other fruits are not needed for this comparison.
x-m-e4-09.s.s2.prompt: In Class 가's graph one unit of the scale is 2 students, and in Class 나's graph one unit is 5 students. Find 2 different numbers of units of the tangerine bar at which the number of students who like tangerines is the same in the two classes. (Bars can be drawn up to 20 units. Number of units for Class 가 a, number of units for Class 나 b)
x-m-e4-09.s.s2.hint.0: For each class, write the number of students as 'number of units × students per unit.'
x-m-e4-09.s.s2.hint.1: Change the number of units for Class 나 as 1, 2, 3... and fit the number of units for Class 가 to match.
x-m-e4-09.s.s2.hint.2: Calculate to check that the two numbers of students really are the same.
x-m-e4-09.s.s2.var.a: Number of units for Class 가
x-m-e4-09.s.s2.var.b: Number of units for Class 나
x-m-e4-09.s.s2.ok.c1: The number of units is a natural number from 1 to 20.
x-m-e4-09.s.s2.fail.c1: The number of units must be a natural number from 1 to 20.
x-m-e4-09.s.s2.ok.c2: The numbers of students in the two classes are the same.
x-m-e4-09.s.s2.fail.c2: The numbers of students in the two classes are not the same.
x-m-e4-09.s.s2.explain: Class 가 with 5 units is 5×2=10 students, and Class 나 with 2 units is 2×5=10 students. 10 units and 4 units make 20 students, and 15 units and 6 units make 30 students, which are also the same. If the number one unit stands for is different, the number of students can be the same even when the numbers of units are different.
x-m-e4-09.s.s2.because.prompt: Write why the numbers of students can be the same even though the lengths of the bars are different.
x-m-e4-09.s.s2.because.hint.0: Compare the number one unit of the scale stands for in the two graphs.
x-m-e4-09.s.s2.because.hint.1: Multiply the numbers of units you made by the number one unit stands for.
x-m-e4-09.s.s2.because.placeholder: Example: In the two graphs, one unit is ...
x-m-e4-09.s.s2.because.selfAssess.0: Did you change your two numbers of units into numbers of students and say that the same value comes out?
x-m-e4-09.s.s2.because.selfAssess.1: Did you say why you must not compare by bar length alone?
x-m-e4-09.s.s2.because.model.0: One unit stands for a different number of students, so you have to multiply the number of units by the number of students per unit to know the number of students. 5 units × 2 students = 10 students, 2 units × 5 students = 10 students.
x-m-e4-09.s.s2.because.model.1: The size of one unit of the scale is different, so you must not compare by bar length alone. You have to multiply the number of units of each bar by how many students one unit stands for, to change it into the number of students.

x-m-e4-10.title: The Pattern of Matchstick Squares
x-m-e4-10.goal: Know that a few values in a table do not decide a pattern as just one, and then revise and apply the pattern after you learn the structure of the shape.
x-m-e4-10.material: You make a shape by joining squares in a row with matchsticks. 4 matchsticks are needed for 1 square, and 7 matchsticks for 2 squares.
x-m-e4-10.thinking.0: Guessing a pattern from little data
x-m-e4-10.thinking.1: Revising your judgment with new information
x-m-e4-10.thinking.2: Applying the pattern to a large number
x-m-e4-10.prereq.0: Finding the relationship between two numbers by looking at a table
x-m-e4-10.s.s1.prompt: Each time more information is added, choose the answer that fits the question.
x-m-e4-10.s.s1.hint.0: Check one by one whether the information at each step matches your earlier guess.
x-m-e4-10.s.s1.hint.1: Think about how to count the 4 matchsticks for 1 square and the 7 for 2 squares by splitting them up to fit the structure.
x-m-e4-10.s.s1.st.0.info: All that has been told so far is two cells of the table. 1 square → 4 matchsticks, 2 squares → 7 matchsticks.
x-m-e4-10.s.s1.st.0.ask: How many matchsticks are there for 3 squares? Choose the most likely guess looking only at the table.
x-m-e4-10.s.s1.st.0.after: Two cells alone do not decide the pattern as just one. Both 10 and 11 are guesses that fit the table. You need more information about the shape.
x-m-e4-10.s.s1.st.0.o.a: 10 matchsticks. It goes up by 3 each time one square is added
x-m-e4-10.s.s1.st.0.r.a: You found the pattern from the difference of the two values. There are only two cells so far, so leave open that there could be another pattern.
x-m-e4-10.s.s1.st.0.o.b: 11 matchsticks. The amount it goes up gets bigger by one each time: 3, 4, 5
x-m-e4-10.s.s1.st.0.r.b: This guessed a different pattern from two cells. It is possible, but right now there is no way to check it.
x-m-e4-10.s.s1.st.0.r.c: With 2 squares it should be 8, but it is actually 7. Check whether it matches the table.
x-m-e4-10.s.s1.st.1.info: The squares are joined one at a time to the right, and each new square shares one side with the square before it. So each new square needs only 3 more matchsticks.
x-m-e4-10.s.s1.st.1.ask: Taking this information into account, how many matchsticks are there for 3 squares and for 4 squares?
x-m-e4-10.s.s1.st.1.after: Each newly joined square adds 3, so it is 10 with 3 squares and 13 with 4 squares. Of the first two guesses, the guess that it always goes up by 3 was right.
x-m-e4-10.s.s1.st.1.r.a: This followed the guess that the amount it goes up gets bigger, but the new information says it is always 3.
x-m-e4-10.s.s1.st.1.r.c: This calculated 4 for every square. Take into account the information that one side is shared.
x-m-e4-10.s.s1.st.1.r.d: It is right for 3 squares, but for 4 squares the amount it went up is not 3.
x-m-e4-10.s.s1.st.2.info: Now you want to join 10 squares.
x-m-e4-10.s.s1.st.2.after: The first square takes 4 matchsticks, and each of the other 9 squares adds 3 more, so 4+3×9=31. What matters is that only the first one takes 4 and the others take 3 each.
x-m-e4-10.s.s1.st.2.r.a: The first square needs 4 matchsticks. Think about the first one and the ones joined later separately.
x-m-e4-10.s.s1.st.2.r.b: Sides are shared, so 4 each are not needed.
x-m-e4-10.s.s1.st.2.o.c: 31 matchsticks. Start with 4 for the first square and add 3 more, 9 times
x-m-e4-10.s.s1.st.2.o.d: 37 matchsticks. Start with 7 and add 3 more, 10 times
x-m-e4-10.s.s1.st.2.r.d: 7 matchsticks is for 2 squares. How many more times do you add to get to 10 squares?
x-m-e4-10.s.s1.reflect: How did your thinking change between looking at only two cells of the table and knowing the information about the shape? How is it different when it is okay to decide a pattern from the table alone and when it is not?
x-m-e4-10.s.s2.prompt: Using the pattern you found, make 2 different cases in which you join more than 10 squares but use at most 50 matchsticks. (number of squares n, number of matchsticks y)
x-m-e4-10.s.s2.hint.0: Pick a number of squares and find the number of matchsticks needed by the pattern.
x-m-e4-10.s.s2.hint.1: First estimate the largest number of squares that does not go over 50 matchsticks.
x-m-e4-10.s.s2.fail.c1: The number of squares must be a natural number greater than 10.
x-m-e4-10.s.s2.ok.c2: The number of matchsticks fits the pattern.
x-m-e4-10.s.s2.fail.c2: The number of matchsticks does not fit the pattern.
x-m-e4-10.s.s2.explain: With 11 squares it is 4+3×10=34 matchsticks, and with 16 squares it is 4+3×15=49 matchsticks. With 17 squares it is 52, which is over 50.
